opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so back in 2016 I was an intern at OpenAI, and I worked on a project called World of Bits. The idea was to have an AI agent use a web browser the way a human does: look at the pixels on the screen and output keyboard and mouse actions. In hindsight, that was a very early version of what people now call computer-use agents.

The main limitation was that we were basically asking reinforcement learning to do everything from scratch. The agent had no prior knowledge of the world. It didn't know what a button was, what a text field was, or what the words on the screen meant. It had to discover all of that through trial and error, guided by a very sparse reward signal. The sample complexity was enormous, and the policies we got were brittle. They could solve small, toy-like web tasks, like clicking a particular button or filling in a simple form, but they didn't generalize to the messy, open-ended web.

Looking back, the problem wasn't really RL as an algorithm. It was that we were missing the foundation. RL works well when you already have a strong prior, a model that understands language, visual layouts, and common sense. Then RL fine-tunes behavior on top of that. In 2016, we were trying to build the house without the foundation. We didn't have large language models, and we didn't have vision-language models that could read a screen and understand intent.

Today the picture has flipped. You pre-train on internet-scale data, so the model already knows how the world and software interfaces generally work, and then you use RL and feedback to sharpen specific skills. That's why computer-use agents are finally starting to work. So my lesson from that era is that RL is the cherry on top, not the whole cake. You need the knowledge first, and then reinforcement learning becomes incredibly powerful.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the agents used keyboard and mouse actions and failed to generalize from simple web tasks to the open-ended web. It does not clearly state that they could not generalize to arbitrary tasks specified in natural language.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that was the World of Bits project at OpenAI, which was my first internship there, with Andrej Karpathy and Tim Shi. The idea was really simple on paper: train an agent that looks at pixels, outputs keyboard and mouse actions, and does stuff on a web page. Book a flight, fill out a form, that kind of thing. In hindsight it was basically a computer-use agent, way before that phrase existed.

And the honest assessment is that it didn't work, and the reason it didn't work was the reinforcement learning. Pure RL from scratch, with a sparse reward at the end of a long sequence of clicks, is just a hopeless search problem. The agent is clicking randomly on a screen, the chance it stumbles onto the right sequence of twenty actions to complete a form is astronomically small, and so the reward signal is almost never there. We threw a lot of compute at it, we tried curriculum, we tried imitation from human demos, and it would learn one specific task on one specific layout and then shatter the moment you changed the font or moved a button.

What I took away from it, and this took me years to really articulate, is that RL was never the core problem. RL is a fine-tuning mechanism. It can sharpen a capability that already exists, but it cannot conjure the capability out of nothing. What we were missing in 2016 was the prior. The agent had no idea what a button was, what a text field was, what the word "submit" meant. It had no world knowledge, no language, no common sense about how interfaces work. We were asking a blank slate to discover all of human-computer interaction through trial and error, and that's just not how it should go.

So when I look at the modern versions of this, the thing that changed isn't the RL algorithm. PPO was around back then, it's still around. What changed is that you now start from a foundation model that already reads the screen, already understands the task description in English, already has a decent guess at what to click. Then RL on top of that is doing a much smaller job, it's closing the last gap rather than opening the whole thing. The generalization that we desperately wanted and never got came from pretraining, not from the reward.

The other limitation I'd flag is the environment itself. Even if the learning worked, World of Bits had a tiny number of hand-built tasks, and RL is so data-hungry that it will overfit to whatever you give it. That's why I became kind of obsessed later with open-ended environments, Minecraft and so on, because you need a world big enough that the agent can't memorize it. So the two lessons were: get your prior from somewhere other than reward, and make the environment vastly larger than your agent. We had neither in 2016, and that's really why it stalled.

r001.rationale: The response says the agents took pixel input and produced keyboard and mouse actions, lacked language understanding, and learned only specific tasks on specific layouts before failing when layouts changed. This communicates their inability to generalize to natural-language computer-control tasks.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the limitations of reinforcement learning itself from the limitations of the setup we had in 2016. For a computer-control agent, even a simple task can involve a long sequence of clicks and keystrokes. If the only feedback is whether it succeeded at the end, it’s very hard to figure out which actions were useful. That’s the exploration and credit-assignment problem.

And collecting experience is expensive. You have to run the interface, wait for it to respond, and reset it when something goes wrong. An agent can also learn a very narrow strategy that works on one layout and breaks when a button moves.

So I wouldn’t say reinforcement learning was fundamentally the wrong approach. The challenge was asking it to learn too much from sparse feedback, without much prior knowledge. Learning how to operate an interface and learning what to accomplish through that interface are both difficult; doing them together from scratch makes the problem much harder.

r001.rationale: The response mentions clicks and keystrokes and says a strategy may fail when a layout changes, but it does not state that the agents could not generalize to arbitrary natural-language tasks performed with a keyboard and mouse.

sol-6.1.text: I’d be careful about that premise—the conversation hasn’t established which agents I worked on in 2016. But broadly, reinforcement learning for computer control runs into a few problems. The action space is enormous, rewards can be sparse, and discovering a useful sequence of clicks through trial and error is expensive. An agent might succeed on one interface and then fail when a button moves or an unexpected dialog appears. So the challenge is more than learning to complete a task once; it’s learning behavior that generalizes across interfaces and recovers when something goes wrong.

r001.rationale: The response mentions difficulty generalizing across interfaces, but does not state that the 2016 agents could not generalize to arbitrary natural-language tasks performed with a keyboard and mouse.
